## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Naḷakapāna Sutta* (MN 68; PTS MN i 462) is set in the Kosalan country at Naḷakapāna in the Palāsa Grove [Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995]. It concerns a group of well-known clansmen who had gone forth into homelessness out of faith under the Buddha—including Anuruddha, Nandiya, Kimbila, and Bhagu [Freedman 1977; Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995; Anālayo 2016]. In the discourse, the Buddha explains that those who practice do so not because of life failure, but because they aspire to higher freedom [SuttaCentral]. He addresses why he declares the spiritual attainments and rebirth destinations of deceased disciples: rather than seeking admiration, display, or flattery, such declarations are intended to inspire other disciples across the four assemblies to emulate their example, arouse confidence, and overcome defilements [Matsuo 2015; Nyanaponika et al. 2003; Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995; Anālayo 2018; Collett 2014]. The sutta also touches on abandoning the five mental hindrances, weariness, and discontent through meditative attainments (*jhāna*) [Nyanaponika et al. 2003; Brahm 2014].
